title: What a logo does — Image Wiki
text:
What a logo does
  A mark has one job — to identify one thing and tell it apart from everything else. It does not explain the business and it cannot make the business good; the meaning runs the other way.

  
    Termlogo / mark / trademark
    Also calledmark, trademark, logotype, brand mark
    Not the same asbrand, visual identity, trademark registration
    Read7 min
  

  
    
      On this page
      
        The meaning runs inwardSix shapes the same job takesAn emblem is a different objectThe mark is not the brandCommon mistakes
      
    
  

  Look at your phone's home screen. Two dozen rounded squares, each about a centimetre across, and you can land a finger on the one you want before you have read any of the labels. You are not reading. You are matching shapes, from memory, at a glance.
That is the whole job of a logo, and it is a smaller job than most people expect. A logo identifies. It picks one thing out of a crowd of similar things and says: this one. It does not have to explain what the thing does, argue that the thing is good, or be liked.
Paul Rand wrote the flattest version of this in 1991. A logo is a flag, a signature, an escutcheon. It does not sell, it identifies. It is rarely a description of a business. And it "derives its meaning from the quality of the thing it symbolizes, not the other way around" (ID-001).
The meaning runs inward
A new mark is empty. Nobody has seen it, so it means nothing, and no amount of drawing will change that on day one. Rand: "It is foolhardy to believe that a logo will do its job right off, before an audience has been properly conditioned."
What fills it is everything the viewer later experiences while the mark is attached. The three-pointed Mercedes star has nothing to do with cars. Lacoste's reptile has nothing to do with shirts, and a bat has nothing to do with rum, but Bacardi is still drunk. Rand calls the Rolls-Royce emblem's design commonplace and says what makes it distinguished is the car. Then he gives the argument its dark half: the swastika was one of the most benign symbols in use until what it came to identify destroyed it, and the drawing itself never changed.


Pure geometry
Script and a sabre


Rand's own pair of examples (ID-001). Both public domain, via Wikimedia Commons.
Left: three vertical bands. No picture, no letters, nothing to interpret. Right: a line of Arabic script above a sabre, dense enough that you cannot resolve it at 50 metres. Two opposite ideas of what a mark should be, and both identify perfectly, because in each case a population learned it.
Rand's point about flags is that this settles the argument about beauty: "The ugliest flag is beautiful if it happens to be on your side." What you feel when you look at a mark is mostly what you already feel about the thing behind it.


So "does this logo communicate innovation and trust?" is close to unanswerable, and it is the question most people reach for first. The answerable questions are narrower and harder: can you tell it apart from its neighbours, can you remember it tomorrow, and can it be reproduced everywhere it has to appear. Rand names only two requirements as mandatory — that a logo be reproducible in one colour, and at exceedingly small sizes.
Six shapes the same job takes
The vocabulary is worth getting straight, because people use these words as if they were rankings.

NORTHGATEWordmarkthe whole name, drawn onceFedEx, Braun, GoogleNGFLettermarkthe initials, set as lettersIBM, BBC, HBOMonogramletters fused into one figureVW, Chanel, Louis VuittonPictorial symbola picture of a real thingApple, Shell, the WWF pandaAbstract symbolmeans nothing until taughtChase, Mitsubishi, PepsiNORTHGATEFERRIESEmblemname sealed inside the shapeStarbucks, NFL, city seals

One invented company, six ways to identify it. None is more advanced than another; they fail differently.
A wordmark and a lettermark carry the name, so they need no teaching — but they must be read, which means they die at distance and in a small square. A monogram trades legibility for compactness. A pictorial symbol is remembered fast and can be described over the phone. An abstract symbol means nothing until an audience is taught it, which costs years and money, and in exchange it is never generic. An emblem locks name and picture into one shape, which looks authoritative and cannot be split, resized small, or used as an app icon.


Put the mark next to the organisation's full name and you get a third thing, which identity manuals call a signature. Canada's Federal Identity Program defines it exactly that way: the combination of a symbol and a title (ID-008-c3). GOV.UK runs a two-part version, a wordmark as the primary identifier with a crown beside it as a supporting element (ID-013-c5). Which combinations are allowed, and how far apart the parts sit, belongs to the system around the mark rather than to the mark.



NASA Graphics Standards Manual, 1976, p. 1.2 (ID-006). Work of the US federal government, public domain.
Two signatures, not two logos. Top: the logotype with the agency name under it in Helvetica Light. Bottom: the same, plus a centre name in the heavier Helvetica Medium — the manual says the bolder weight is what makes the centre name read first even though the agency always comes above it. The mark is identical in both. Everything that changed is the words locked to it.


An emblem is a different object
NASA in 1976 owned two marks at once and refused to let them meet.



NASA Graphics Standards Manual, 1976, p. 1.9 (ID-006). A US Government work, so the document itself carries no copyright.
The seal: a ring of type around a stippled planet, a hairline orbit and a scatter of stars. Count the separate elements, then compare with the four solid letters of the logotype on the same desk. The manual reserves the seal for award presentations and ceremonial events, and states that it should never be used alongside the logotype, because the two "are intended for different purposes and are visually incompatible when seen side by side."
That is the emblem trade-off, written by people who had to enforce it. Detail buys gravity and costs you every small application.


The mark is not the brand
The mark is a few square centimetres. The brand is everything a person has experienced: the queue, the price, the smell of the shop, the hold music, the friend who said it was rubbish. The mark is the handle that retrieves all of it, which is why changing it does not change any of it. Rand allows that a redesign may imply something new, then adds that this "is short-lived if a company doesn't live up to its claim." He also notes that ABC toyed with updating its 1962 mark and dropped the idea after a survey showed how high audience recognition already was — recognition being the one asset a redesign spends.
Common mistakes

"A good logo explains what the company does." Almost none of the ones you can name do. Rand goes further: appropriateness is desirable but a one-to-one relation between symbol and thing symbolised is often impossible and sometimes objectionable.
"Our logo is our brand." Then a competitor could copy the mark and take the brand with it, which is plainly not what happens.
"It's a registered trademark, so it's a strong mark." Two unrelated properties. NASA's insignia is protected by law under 14 CFR 1221 (ID-007); the protection says nothing about whether it reads at 16 pixels.
"I don't like it, so it is bad." Likes and dislikes, Rand says, should play no part in the problem of identification. Ask instead whether you could pick it out of nine competitors.
"The mark should look modern." Modern dates. Rand lists durability and timelessness among the things effectiveness actually depends on, alongside distinctiveness, visibility, usability, memorability and universality.


Reading a mark in five seconds

Cover the name. Do you still know whose it is? If not, it is a piece of lettering, not yet a mark.
Name what it depicts, then name what the organisation does. Unrelated is normal, not a fault.
Which of the six kinds is it — wordmark, lettermark, monogram, pictorial, abstract, emblem? That tells you which failures to go looking for.
Ask what is doing the identifying: the shape, the colour, or the words. Only the shape survives a fax and a favicon.
Blur your eyes until detail is gone (How to look at an image). Whatever silhouette is left is what people actually store, because the eye groups big shapes well before it resolves detail (Gestalt grouping).
